forecasts.rationale: Our central estimate is $0.77 per MHz-pop, about $41B of bids for 160 MHz. That is below the lower C-band's own $0.87 on the same 335M-pop basis and close to the 3.45 GHz auction's $0.70. Each of the three carriers already holds about 150 MHz or more of mid-band, winners owe about $16B of clearing and altimeter costs on top of their bids (about $0.30 per MHz-pop), and AT&T is stretched after paying $23B for EchoStar spectrum. A serious SpaceX bid is the main upside. The range is wide because US auctions have missed consensus in both directions.
forecasts.drivers_up: SpaceX bids seriously as a fourth bidder; Verizon or AT&T fight for blocks next to their existing C-band to build a 440 MHz contiguous range; carriers bid defensively after SpaceX's spectrum moves; little other new mid-band arrives before 2030.
forecasts.drivers_down: About $16B of add-on costs; carrier debt (AT&T at 3.13x leverage, Verizon net debt $123.7B); Verizon's 4-5 year deployment lag; T-Mobile will only buy if cheaper than adding sites; the 2.7 GHz band follows in 2028; second tranches abroad cleared far lower (Canada 3800 MHz about 90% below 3500 MHz).
forecasts.base_rate: US mid-band auctions in 2021-22 cleared $0.70-0.87 per MHz-pop on 335M pops; the 2015 AWS-3 peak was about $2.70. Analyst ranges (TD Cowen $30-75B, Carr $30-60B) imply $0.56-1.40. Five of the last eight big US auctions beat consensus, while 600 MHz and 2.5 GHz fell well short.
forecasts.signposts: Auction 115 short-form filings (6-20 January 2027), especially whether SpaceX applies; the qualified-bidder list and upfront payments (around March 2027); bidding pace in the first weeks after the 27 April 2027 start.

forecasts.rationale: Proceeds are the price forecast times 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz times 335M people), so about $41B at the middle. That sits inside Carr's $30-60B and TD Cowen's $30-75B ranges and far below the $81B raised for 280 MHz in 2021. If only the three carriers bid, and they hold back, proceeds land near $30B. If SpaceX bids hard, they land near $50B or more. The $72B top end allows for a surprise like the 2021 auction, which beat its forecast by 55-100%.
forecasts.drivers_up: SpaceX or another new bidder; carriers paying up for blocks next to their C-band; a scarcity of other mid-band before 2030; strategic bidding to keep SpaceX out.
forecasts.drivers_down: Only three committed bidders for eight blocks per market, which invites restraint; $16B of add-on costs; stretched balance sheets after the EchoStar deals; the FCC's refusal to give satellite coverage buildout credit, which deters SpaceX.
forecasts.base_rate: Lower C-band ($81B) beat its $40-52B consensus. 3.45 GHz landed near consensus. 600 MHz (about half of forecasts) and 2.5 GHz (well below $1-5B estimates) fell short.
forecasts.signposts: Whether SpaceX appears on the Auction 115 qualified-bidder list (early 2027); daily round results after 27 April 2027; gross bids passing $50.4B, the level that beats the 2021 price per MHz-pop.

forecasts.rationale: We expect big 2029-30 deals to have a median near $0.90 per MHz-pop, below today's $1.40 AT&T-EchoStar benchmark. The likely deal set mixes cheap FCC auctions (2.7 GHz, 1675/2020 MHz, perhaps 4.4 or 7 GHz, at roughly $0.3-0.8) with dearer private sales of low-band and paired spectrum ($1.2-2.5). By 2030 mid-band supply is up about a third, which pushes generic mid-band down while low-band keeps its premium. With only a handful of qualifying deals, which deals happen decides the median, so the range is wide.
forecasts.drivers_up: Private low-band or paired sales dominate the sample; SpaceX and Amazon keep buying; 2.7 GHz or 7 GHz auctions slip past 2030; traffic re-accelerates on AI uplink.
forecasts.drivers_down: Several FCC auctions land in 2029-30 with federal exclusion zones and lots of MHz; carriers have room after upper C-band; SpaceX says its portfolio is complete; foreign mid-band prices keep falling.
forecasts.base_rate: 2021-22 US auctions cleared $0.67-0.87 per MHz-pop; 2025-26 private sales ran $0.52-2.53 with a median near $1.20. Real US mid-band prices have fallen since 2015 as supply rose. Recent European mid-band averages are about $0.07.
forecasts.signposts: The FCC's 2.7 GHz auction date and result (Carr targets 2028); the price of EchoStar's paired AWS-3 sale (promised by September 2028); any SpaceX or Amazon low-band purchase in 2028-30.

forecasts.rationale: We expect one spectrum-only deal of $5B or more in 2027-30, with roughly a one-in-three chance of none. The most likely is EchoStar's paired AWS-3 remainder, marked near $8B, which EchoStar has promised to sell by September 2028, though it could be split into smaller pieces. Further buying by SpaceX or Amazon, or a carrier sale or swap after Auction 115, could add one or two more. Before 2025 such deals came about once every five years; the 2025-26 burst came from one forced seller and one new buyer.
forecasts.drivers_up: SpaceX or Amazon want more terrestrial spectrum; EchoStar sells its AWS-3 in one block; Anterix or Ligado assets get re-rated; post-auction swaps between carriers.
forecasts.drivers_down: Few large nationwide holdings remain outside the big three; SpaceX called 800 MHz its last critical piece; FCC concentration review; auctions offer an alternative supply route; EchoStar may sell in pieces under $5B.
forecasts.base_rate: About 0.2 qualifying deals a year in 2013-24; three in 2025-26 (AT&T and SpaceX from EchoStar, SpaceX from Grain).
forecasts.signposts: An EchoStar paired AWS-3 sale announcement (deadline September 2028); SpaceX comments on spectrum needs after Grain closes (mid-2027); Amazon's terrestrial spectrum plans once Globalstar closes (2027).

forecasts.rationale: We expect about 330 EB in 2030, roughly double 2025's 159 EB, with yearly growth fading from 20% to about 12% (about 15.5% a year on average). Bottom-up, phones at about 37 GB a month give about 150 EB, and about 28M fixed wireless lines at about 520 GB a month give about 175 EB. Mature markets show the same slowdown (UK +18%, Switzerland 20-25%), and 82-89% of phone data still rides Wi-Fi. The top of the range is CTIA's own 22%-a-year path, which industry forecasts have usually overshot.
forecasts.drivers_up: Fixed wireless grows toward 30M+ lines on upper C-band capacity; multimodal AI and glasses add uplink; robotaxi fleets scale; video quality rises.
forecasts.drivers_down: Fixed wireless adds keep slowing (Verizon 159K in Q3 2026 vs 261K); fiber overbuild by the same carriers; Wi-Fi offload; a saturated phone base; better video compression.
forecasts.base_rate: Growth fell from 38% (2022) to 20% (2025). Ericsson forecasts 13% a year for North American smartphone data to 2031. Mature markets settle in the high teens or below.
forecasts.signposts: Ericsson Mobility Report (30 November 2026 and June 2027); CTIA's survey of 2026 traffic (around September 2027); quarterly fixed wireless net adds from Verizon and AT&T.

forecasts.rationale: We extend the 2030 path at about 10% a year, giving about 525 EB in 2035, roughly 3.3 times 2025. Every maturing market shows growth decaying, and Ericsson's own forecast slows to 14% by 2031. The range is wide and skewed up. The low end has growth near 6% after a weak 2030; the high end keeps growth near 16% on uplink-heavy AI devices, 6G and 7 GHz capacity.
forecasts.drivers_up: Physical AI (robotaxis, drones, delivery robots) on wide-area networks; AI glasses and camera assistants; 7 GHz and 6G capacity making fixed wireless cheaper.
forecasts.drivers_down: Fixed wireless shrinks under fiber overbuild; phone use plateaus; on-device AI cuts round trips; Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz unlicensed absorb more indoor traffic.
forecasts.base_rate: Ericsson has repeatedly cut its forecasts (its 2030 global figure fell from 473 to 430 EB a month in one year). CTIA's 4x-by-2032 path (about 640 EB) sits above our 2032 range.
forecasts.signposts: CTIA growth in 2027-28 (holding above 15% would lift this); US uplink share in Ookla and Opensignal data; robotaxi fleet counts (Waymo about 4,000 in September 2026).

forecasts.rationale: The only measurement is 0.06% of mobile traffic (Ericsson, April 2025). Reaching our 1.5% median by 2030 needs AI traffic to grow about 120% a year while total traffic grows 15-18%. Text AI is light, much inference runs on the device or server to server, and glasses and indoor robots mostly ride the phone or Wi-Fi. The upper tail is fat because camera and voice assistants and AI video apps could scale the way TikTok did, and the vendors who publish the measurement have reasons to count AI traffic broadly.
forecasts.drivers_up: Always-on multimodal assistants; AI glasses (IDC sees 27M display-less units by 2030); AI video generation apps being counted; robotaxi uplink; generous vendor definitions.
forecasts.drivers_down: On-device models; AI features folded into existing apps and not counted separately; Wi-Fi offload; robots on Wi-Fi or private 5G indoors.
forecasts.base_rate: Broad-definition forecasts (GSMA 5-20% by 2030, Nokia 44% of all traffic by 2035) have a record of overshooting. Video took over a decade to reach about 75% of mobile traffic; TikTok reached double-digit share in about four years.
forecasts.signposts: Any new operator or vendor AI traffic measurement (watch Ericsson's 30 November 2026 and June 2027 reports); AI glasses shipments in 2027; robotaxi fleet sizes and per-vehicle data use.

forecasts.rationale: We expect about 29M fixed wireless homes and businesses across the big three at end-2030, up from about 19M in Q3 2026. Net adds have already peaked (3.8M in 2025, about 3.6M in 2026), and we assume they keep decaying toward 2M a year. That lands close to the carriers' own targets: T-Mobile 15M by 2030, Verizon 'well beyond' 8-9M by 2028, AT&T about 5M. New Street's estimate of about 32M of Big 3 capacity caps the upside unless upper C-band adds room.
forecasts.drivers_up: Upper C-band capacity from 2028-30; cable broadband price rises; AT&T's EchoStar 3.45 GHz enabling more Internet Air; steady T-Mobile adds.
forecasts.drivers_down: Rising disconnects as the base grows; AT&T and Verizon pushing fiber first; carriers rationing capacity for mobile; satellite broadband competition; slower speeds at peak hours.
forecasts.base_rate: Product S-curves flatten once 50-70% of capacity is used. Industry adds fell from 3.8M (2025) to about 3.6M (2026), and Verizon's Q3 2026 adds fell 39% year on year.
forecasts.signposts: Quarterly fixed wireless net adds (Verizon and AT&T; T-Mobile stopped disclosing in 2026); any FWA price rises or sales pauses; the pace of upper C-band deployment after 2028.

forecasts.rationale: This is our revenue forecast ($266B) divided by our traffic forecast (328 EB), about $0.80 per GB in 2030 against $1.48 in 2025. That is a fall of about 11% a year, half the 2020-25 pace, because traffic growth is slowing while revenue still grows 2-3%. Traffic uncertainty drives nearly all of the range. Even our high case keeps falling every year, so this does not point to a capacity squeeze.
forecasts.drivers_up: Slower traffic growth; carrier price rises; premium tiers for satellite, slicing or AI; carriers rationing cheap fixed wireless.
forecasts.drivers_down: Faster traffic growth from fixed wireless and AI; cable free lines and SpaceX pricing; satellite service bundled free; flat revenue.
forecasts.base_rate: Revenue per GB fell from $412 (2010) to $4.50 (2020) and $1.48 (2025), about -20% a year since 2020. CTIA reports price per MB fell 21% in 2025.
forecasts.signposts: CTIA's annual revenue and traffic figures (each September); the BLS wireless price index after carrier price rises; any slowdown in fixed wireless selling.

forecasts.rationale: Upper C-band (160 MHz) is close to certain and sets the floor. Our central case adds the 2.7 GHz band (about 210 MHz), which has approved federal relocation plans and a 2028 FCC target, for about 370 MHz. The 25 MHz 1675/2020 MHz band is roughly a coin flip. The top of the range needs a 7 GHz or 4.4 GHz auction to finish by 2030, which we put at about 30%, because US mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years from their first target.
forecasts.drivers_up: Statutory deadline of 200 MHz of federal spectrum auctioned by July 2029; Carr's 2028 auction slate (2.7 GHz, 1.6 GHz, 7 GHz); NTIA claims to be ahead of schedule; fiscal need for auction revenue.
forecasts.drivers_down: Defense Department resistance and relocation costs; FAA altimeter issues; NTIA study slips; litigation; once 300 MHz is auctioned, the law stops forcing more until 2033; political change after 2028.
forecasts.base_rate: About 585 MHz was auctioned in 2015-22 (about 73 MHz a year), then none during the 2023-25 lapse in authority. US mid-band auctions have typically slipped 1-3 years.
forecasts.signposts: NTIA's 7.125-7.4 GHz report (due 10 December 2026); FCC 2.7 GHz rules and auction date (2027-28); a final order on 1675/2020 MHz after the October 2026 proposal.

forecasts.rationale: The 2025 law sets an 800 MHz pipeline with at least 300 MHz auctioned by 2034, and our central case delivers about 640 MHz by 2035. That assumes upper C-band, 2.7 GHz and 7.125-7.4 GHz are done, plus part of 4.4-4.94 GHz about half the time. Statutory spectrum targets are usually met late or in part: about 75% of the 2012 Spectrum Act targets were auctioned within the decade. The law also excludes two big federal bands (3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz), and Defense Department resistance caps the upside.
forecasts.drivers_up: WRC-27 identification of 7 GHz and 4.4 GHz for mobile; 6G demand; auction revenue needs; a possible mmWave auction that adds many MHz cheaply.
forecasts.drivers_down: Defense Department preference for sharing over clearing; excluded bands; FCC auction authority lapsing in September 2034; weak bids reducing the fiscal push; shared and unlicensed alternatives.
forecasts.base_rate: About 75% of Spectrum Act targets were met within a decade. The statutory minimum (300 MHz) is met by upper C-band plus 2.7 GHz alone.
forecasts.signposts: WRC-27 decisions on 4.4-4.8 and 7.125-8.4 GHz (October-November 2027); NTIA's identification of the second federal tranche (due July 2029); progress on the nine 4.4 GHz relocation plans.

forecasts.rationale: SpaceX has about 79 MHz pending: 65 MHz from EchoStar (FCC-approved, closing targeted for 30 November 2027) and 14 MHz of 800 MHz from Grain (awaiting FCC approval). Our median of 88 MHz sits a little above that because at least one modest addition is slightly more likely than not: upper C-band wins (about 45%), EchoStar's paired AWS-3, the 2020-2025 MHz block next to its AWS-4, or 2.7 GHz. The floor near 66 MHz is the case where the Grain deal fails. Musk's description of 800 MHz as the 'last critical piece' keeps the median from going higher.
forecasts.drivers_up: Meaningful upper C-band or 2.7 GHz wins; buying EchoStar's paired AWS-3; buying more low-band; SpaceX added about 79 MHz in 13 months.
forecasts.drivers_down: FCC denial or tough conditions on Grain; an EchoStar closing failure; SpaceX capital going to AI; FCC refusal of satellite buildout credit, which makes auction licences costlier to hold.
forecasts.base_rate: The FCC approved every major 2025-26 spectrum transfer, with conditions. SpaceX went from zero to about 79 MHz agreed in 13 months.
forecasts.signposts: The FCC's Grain decision (petitions due 1 December 2026, decision likely mid-2027); SpaceX's Auction 115 short-form (January 2027) and winnings; the EchoStar closing on 30 November 2027.

forecasts.rationale: Satellite-to-phone revenue is well under $1B today, and we expect about $5B in 2030. Summing by operator: SpaceX wholesale from carrier partners plus any US retail (about $2-2.5B), AST's revenue share with its carrier partners (about $1B), and Apple/Amazon-Globalstar, China and IoT (about $1.5B combined). For scale, the whole legacy satellite-phone industry earns a few billion dollars a year, and carriers mostly bundle satellite service at near-zero extra price. The high end needs broadband-class next-generation service, due from 2027-28, to sell as a paid add-on.
forecasts.drivers_up: Next-generation SpaceX satellites (about 20x per-satellite throughput) from 2027; Amazon entry around 2028; AST's ramp to 100+ satellites; car, IoT and wearable contracts; government deals.
forecasts.drivers_down: Bundling at near-zero price; low willingness to pay outside emergencies; three or four constellations competing; Starship and launch slips.
forecasts.base_rate: Iridium earned $0.87B in 2025; the whole legacy mobile-satellite industry earns a few billion a year. Forecasts for new satellite services have usually overshot.
forecasts.signposts: Any SpaceX disclosure of Starlink Mobile revenue; AST reaching about 45 satellites (target mid-2027) and its 2027 revenue guidance; carrier pricing for satellite add-ons.

forecasts.rationale: We expect about 1M US subscribers billed directly by SpaceX at end-2030, with about a one-in-four chance of essentially none. SpaceX has said it plans its own US service once the EchoStar spectrum closes (targeted for 30 November 2027), and we put about 53% on a launch by end-2028. New entrants grow slowly: cable took about 8 years to reach 24M lines with tens of millions of broadband homes to sell to, and Dish/Boost never scaled on its own. The long upper tail covers a cheap plan bundled with Starlink broadband or buying an existing subscriber base.
forecasts.drivers_up: An early-2028 launch; bundling with Starlink broadband homes; low prices; 800 MHz for indoor coverage; tower access deals; buying a regional carrier or a reseller base.
forecasts.drivers_down: Satellites cannot serve dense indoor demand (over 70% of traffic is indoors); T-Mobile refuses an MVNO; phones need support for new bands; closing delays; SpaceX timelines that slip.
forecasts.base_rate: Cable resellers reached about 1M lines in about 1.5 years and about 24M in about 8 years. Dish/Boost reached about 7M after 5 years, mostly through acquired customers.
forecasts.signposts: A SpaceX consumer plan launch and its price (targeted for early 2028); tower access deals (SpaceX has sought about 80,000 sites); phones shipping in 2027-28 with AWS-4 and 800 MHz support.

forecasts.rationale: We expect about $266B in 2030, up about 2.5% a year from $235B in 2025. Industry revenue has grown about 3% a year in nominal terms since 2007, roughly flat after inflation, even as traffic rose by orders of magnitude. 2026 is firmer (AT&T wireless service +5%, T-Mobile +6-9%), and fixed wireless adds about 0.7 points a year. Cable's free lines, Verizon's falling ARPA and a possible SpaceX price war pull the other way.
forecasts.drivers_up: Price rises in a three-network market; fixed wireless growth; T-Mobile-style ARPA gains (+4%); satellite and premium tiers; IoT lines.
forecasts.drivers_down: Cable free lines (about half of Comcast connects); Verizon ARPA down 1.9%; SpaceX entry; a saturated phone base; falling price per GB.
forecasts.base_rate: 2007-25 nominal growth was about 3% a year; Analysys Mason sees North American service revenue roughly flat to 2030. The $235B base comes from Light Reading citing CTIA; other trackers range $255-326B.
forecasts.signposts: Verizon and T-Mobile ARPA trends each quarter; SpaceX's launch price (2028); CTIA's 2026 revenue figure (around September 2027).

forecasts.rationale: We expect the big three to trade at about 6.9x forward EBITDA at end-2030, the same as today. US incumbent carriers have mostly traded between 6x and 8x, and today's level is close to that long-run average once T-Mobile's old premium is set aside. The market has punished each SpaceX spectrum step (carriers fell 9-13% on 9 October 2026), and an upper C-band and 6G spending cycle around 2030 weighs on cash flow. A takeover bid or rational three-network pricing could lift it above 8x.
forecasts.drivers_up: Spectrum monetised through sales or M&A; a SpaceX or hyperscaler bid for a carrier; disciplined pricing among three networks; T-Mobile regaining some premium if SpaceX's build proves slow.
forecasts.drivers_down: SpaceX entry and price pressure; cable share gains; a 2030 capex cycle; higher interest rates.
forecasts.base_rate: US incumbent telcos have mostly traded at 6-8x. The research weights 2030 states at 50% grind (6-7.5x), 30% price pressure (5-6x) and 20% convergence premium (8x or more).
forecasts.signposts: Carrier share moves on SpaceX milestones (Auction 115, 2028 launch); each carrier's upper C-band spend; T-Mobile's multiple versus AT&T and Verizon.

forecasts.rationale: Charter (including Cox) and Comcast had 24.1M mobile lines in Q3 2026 and added about 3.4M over the prior year. We assume adds decay about 10% a year, giving about 35M at end-2030; a straight-line trend gives about 38.6M. Shrinking cable broadband bases cap how many phone lines can be attached, and about half of Comcast's connects are free lines that may churn when promotions end. Cox's footprint inside Charter and the low-cost reseller model on Verizon's network keep growth going.
forecasts.drivers_up: Free-line promotions; bundling to defend broadband; Cox integration; low mobile penetration of cable homes (about 20%); CBRS offload lowering costs.
forecasts.drivers_down: Broadband losses (Comcast -144K and Charter -233K in Q3 2026); free-line roll-off; carrier retaliation on price; SpaceX as a new low-price rival.
forecasts.base_rate: Cable added a steady 3-3.6M lines a year in 2022-26. Comcast's adds are already slowing (368K in Q3 2026 vs 414K a year earlier).
forecasts.signposts: Quarterly cable mobile adds against the 876K Q3 2026 pace; cable broadband subscriber losses; any change to the Verizon wholesale terms.

forecasts.rationale: Industry network capex has been flat at $29-30B since 2023, after the 5G peak of $39B in 2022. We expect about $31.5B in 2030, as upper C-band deployment and early 6G start to lift spending from the trough, plus about 2.5% a year of inflation. Carriers are in harvest mode: Verizon trimmed its 2026 guide, AT&T cut its long-term outlook and T-Mobile guides about $10B. A return toward $39B needs a 2021-22-style spectrum-driven surge, which sits in our top tail.
forecasts.drivers_up: Upper C-band builds (Verizon says 4-5 years); early 6G or 7 GHz overlays; densification for AI uplink; inflation.
forecasts.drivers_down: Network sharing; capital shifting to fiber; vendor price competition; slowing traffic; heavy spending pushed to 2031-32.
forecasts.base_rate: Past cycles peaked early in each generation then fell 20-30%; the 5G cycle rose 42% from 2018 to 2022, then fell 25% by 2024. 2030 sits near the turn from trough to ramp.
forecasts.signposts: Carrier capex guidance for 2028-29 after Auction 115; the pace of upper C-band deployment; announced 6G build plans.

probabilities.rationale: Bidding starts on 27 April 2027 under final rules, and the law requires the auction by July 2027. Similar auctions with clock and assignment phases took about 10-13 weeks (Auctions 107 and 110), so a normal auction closes around August-September 2027. That leaves about four months of slack. The main risks are litigation, an aviation or satellite dispute that delays the start, a government shutdown, or a long bidding war.
probabilities.signposts: Short-form filings close on schedule (6-20 January 2027); the qualified-bidder list appears (around March 2027); bidding actually opens on 27 April 2027.

probabilities.rationale: On the question's 335M-pop basis the 2021 lower C-band was about $0.87, so beating $0.94 means gross bids above $50.4B. Our price forecast puts about a 32% chance on that if the auction finishes, times about 95% that it finishes by end-2028. Getting there essentially needs SpaceX to bid hard against Verizon, or a fight for blocks next to existing C-band holdings. Heavy add-on costs and carrier balance sheets make it less likely than not.
probabilities.signposts: SpaceX on the qualified-bidder list (early 2027); total upfront payments and bidding eligibility (high eligibility signals demand); gross bids passing $50B in the clock phase.

probabilities.rationale: SpaceX took part in the Auction 115 rulemaking, won small licences in the 2026 AWS-3 re-auction, and has the cash and the stated aim to become a full mobile operator. With 3,248 licences on offer, it could win cheap rural blocks if it enters. Against that, the FCC refused to let satellite coverage count toward buildout, so licences carry ground-network obligations, and Musk called 800 MHz the last critical piece. We put about two-thirds on SpaceX applying and about two-thirds on it winning something if it does.
probabilities.signposts: The public list of short-form applicants (late January 2027); the qualified-bidder list (around March 2027); SpaceX comments on terrestrial plans at its Q4 2026 results.

probabilities.rationale: The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026, the licences have sat in a trust since 22 May 2026, and closing is targeted for 30 November 2027. SpaceX is funding EchoStar's interest through November 2027, which supports that date. The risk is timing: there is only one month of slack before the deadline, and the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless bankruptcy cases add litigation risk. Both sides have strong reasons to close on time.
probabilities.signposts: Any change to the 30 November 2027 target in EchoStar or SpaceX filings; rulings in the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless Chapter 11 cases; SpaceX confirming the $8.5B cash payment ahead of closing.

probabilities.rationale: The FCC accepted the filing on 10 November 2026, with petitions due 1 December and oppositions 8 December. Its informal 180-day review points to a decision around mid-2027, leaving about six months of buffer. This FCC approved every major 2025-26 transfer, including SpaceX-EchoStar in about eight months, and SpaceX holds no other low-band, so the concentration screen does not bind. The remaining risks are public-safety interference objections at 800 MHz, conditions that slow the order, or political friction.
probabilities.signposts: Who files petitions to deny by 1 December 2026 (AT&T, Verizon or public-safety groups); any pause in the FCC's 180-day clock; an order by mid-2027.

probabilities.rationale: SpaceX has told investors it plans a US consumer mobile service on its own spectrum, targeting early 2028, once the EchoStar deal closes around 30 November 2027. Many phones already support Dish's band 70 frequencies, which helps. But that leaves only about 13 months, and SpaceX timelines, next-generation satellite launches and Starship cadence usually slip 6-12 months. A satellite-only or bundled plan billed by SpaceX would also count, which keeps this near a coin flip.
probabilities.signposts: The EchoStar closing on schedule (30 November 2027); the first next-generation direct-to-cell satellite launches (2027); a SpaceX plan announcement, beta or pricing in the first half of 2028.

probabilities.rationale: SpaceX would need to pass the smaller of Charter and Comcast, which we expect at roughly 20-30M lines by 2035. That means 20M or more directly billed subscribers from a launch around 2028. Cable took about 8 years to reach 24M lines with bundles and free lines, Dish never scaled on its own, and satellites cannot carry dense indoor demand. The probability rests mainly on buying a subscriber base or a very cheap plan that scales fast.
probabilities.signposts: SpaceX direct US subscribers at end-2029 (above 3M would raise this sharply); any SpaceX purchase of a carrier or reseller base; large tower or site deals that give it urban coverage.

probabilities.rationale: No non-telecom tech company has bought a US facilities-based carrier in 30 years; Google Fi and others stayed resellers. SpaceX needs towers, operations and customers, and even a small regional carrier would count, which lifts the odds above that base rate. Amazon's Globalstar deal shows appetite for spectrum assets. But Musk's stated approach is to build, not buy, the big three are effectively unbuyable, and cable mobile is core to the broadband bundle.
probabilities.signposts: Whether SpaceX signs tower leases or instead holds M&A talks (2027-28); Amazon's plans after Globalstar closes and its satellite-to-phone launch (around 2028); strategic reviews at regional carriers.

probabilities.rationale: For revenue per GB to rise, traffic growth would have to fall below revenue growth of about 2-4% in some year. CTIA traffic growth has not been below 14% since at least 2010, and our central path stays at 12-18% through 2030. Even our slow case keeps growth near 8-10%. The remaining chance is mostly a CTIA method change, such as splitting out fixed wireless, or carriers sharply throttling fixed wireless.
probabilities.signposts: CTIA traffic growth in each September survey from 2027; BLS wireless price index after carrier price rises; any carrier pausing fixed wireless sales.

probabilities.rationale: US traffic growth fell from 38% in 2022 to 20% in 2025, and our central path keeps it at 12-18% for 2027-30. A year above 25% needs a new driver: cheap fixed wireless on new upper C-band capacity, an AI uplink surge, or a CTIA method change. The series has jumped 12 points or more three times since 2018, and four annual chances keep this from being negligible. The research team's own estimate was 15%.
probabilities.signposts: CTIA's 2026 growth figure (around September 2027); Ericsson's North American growth readings; fixed wireless adds re-accelerating once upper C-band is deployed (2028-30).

probabilities.rationale: 3GPP's Release 21 final spec freeze is March 2029. The first US 5G launch came about 10-13 months after its freeze and LTE about 21 months, so a first 6G launch lands between late 2029 and late 2030, right at the deadline. T-Mobile says it will be first around 2030, Ericsson expects first commercial systems in 2030, and a small paid launch for marketing would count. Against that are flat capex, weak returns, no new 7 GHz spectrum by 2030, and any 3GPP slip.
probabilities.signposts: The Release 21 stage-3 freeze holding at December 2028; 6G chipset and handset announcements for 2029-30; carrier 6G trial and launch announcements.

probabilities.rationale: The candidates are 7.125-7.4 GHz (NTIA report due 10 December 2026) and part of 4.4-4.94 GHz (nine relocation plans under review). Carr wants 7 GHz on a 2028 auction slate, but the 2.7 GHz band alone can meet the law's 2029 federal deadline, which removes pressure for upper mid-band until 2033. Federal study-to-auction has taken from about 14-17 months (3.45 GHz) to about a decade (CBRS), and mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years. WRC-27 decisions also take effect only in 2029.
probabilities.signposts: NTIA's 7 GHz report findings (10 December 2026); an FCC 7 GHz proposal and auction date (2027-28); the WRC-27 outcome on 7.125-8.4 GHz and 4.4-4.8 GHz (November 2027).

probabilities.rationale: EchoStar told the FCC it would sell its remaining licences by September 2028 in return for buildout waivers, its paired AWS-3 is marked near $8B, and Verizon has held talks. That alone makes a sale about 60-75% likely. Array's retained C-band, Anterix's strategic review after its band was widened, and NextNav add independent chances. Only four or five buyers exist, and a partial sale may not count as 'most', which keeps this below 90%.
probabilities.signposts: An EchoStar paired AWS-3 sale agreement (watch 2027 to September 2028); the outcome of Anterix's strategic review; FCC action on NextNav's lower 900 MHz petition.

probabilities.rationale: Over most four-year windows since 2010, an equal-weight basket of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile has lagged the S&P 500; it mainly won when the market fell. Today the carriers start cheap (about 6.9x EBITDA after the SpaceX sell-off) with 4-6% dividend yields, while the S&P is richly valued and heavy in AI stocks. SpaceX entry, cable share gains and a 2030 spending cycle are structural headwinds. Large tracking error makes this closer to a coin flip than the base rate alone, but still tilted to No.
probabilities.signposts: SpaceX's launch and pricing (2028); any sharp AI-led fall in the S&P 500; carrier ARPA trends and cable share gains each quarter.

scenarios.name: Steady grind
scenarios.tagline: Spectrum keeps its value, but nobody gets a re-rating.
scenarios.summary: Defined as: SpaceX bills fewer than 3M US mobile lines directly at end-2030, and the median 2029-30 deal price is $0.60-1.40 per MHz-pop. Upper C-band clears near $0.65-0.95 ($35-50B), mostly to the three carriers. Traffic roughly doubles to about 300-350 EB, fixed wireless reaches about 29M lines, and revenue per GB keeps falling about 10% a year. SpaceX closes its EchoStar and Grain deals and launches a modest service, but stays a niche operator, and upper mid-band auctions slip past 2030.
scenarios.spectrum_prices: Mid-band trades near today's range of roughly $0.6-1.4 per MHz-pop. Low-band keeps a premium of about $1.2-2.0 because no new low-band is coming.
scenarios.carriers: Revenue grows 2-3% a year and multiples stay at about 6-7.5x. Returns come from dividends and buybacks, not from spectrum value.
scenarios.satellites: Satellite-to-phone grows into a few-billion-dollar bundled add-on. SpaceX is a coverage layer and a buyer, not a price-setter.
scenarios.investors: Spectrum exposure pays only through events, such as EchoStar's remainder sale or an Anterix or Array exit. Carrier stocks are income holdings, not a spectrum bet.
scenarios.signposts: Auction 115 gross bids between $35B and $50B (2027); fixed wireless adds below 3M a year from 2027; SpaceX direct US lines below 1M at end-2029.

scenarios.name: Supply wave
scenarios.tagline: The spectrum law works, supply floods in, and prices per MHz-pop fall.
scenarios.summary: Defined as: SpaceX bills fewer than 3M US lines directly at end-2030, and the median 2029-30 deal price is below $0.60 per MHz-pop. Upper C-band clears low, near $0.40-0.65 ($22-35B), as three carriers split 160 MHz with little contest. NTIA and the FCC move fast: 2.7 GHz in 2028 and a 7 GHz or 4.4 GHz auction by 2030 take new supply past 430 MHz. Traffic growth fades toward 10%, Wi-Fi keeps most phone data, and new auctions clear at $0.3-0.6, echoing Canada's second mid-band tranche.
scenarios.spectrum_prices: The mid-band deal median falls below $0.60 and keeps falling in real terms. Low-band holds up better at about $1.0-1.6.
scenarios.carriers: Capacity gets cheap, which helps margins and fixed wireless, but price competition and cable keep revenue growth near 1-2%. Multiples sit around 6-7x.
scenarios.satellites: Satellite sharing of carrier spectrum and new auction bands with satellite rights reduce the need to own spectrum. Only the few dedicated satellite bands keep strategic value.
scenarios.investors: Pure-play spectrum holders lose, because sale prices fall and buyers have alternatives. Towers and equipment makers gain more from new deployments than holders do.
scenarios.signposts: A favourable NTIA 7 GHz report (10 December 2026) followed by an FCC 7 GHz auction date in 2028 or earlier; Auction 115 gross bids under $35B (2027); a 2.7 GHz auction clearing below $0.50.
scenarios.forecast_links: q_ucb_price $0.40-0.65; q_ucb_proceeds $22-35B; q_midband_2030 under $0.60; q_new_mhz_2030 435-680 MHz; b_7ghz Yes; q_traffic_2030 260-310 EB; q_rev_per_gb $0.85-1.04; b_ucb_above No; q_bigdeals 0-1; q_new_mhz_2035 above 640 MHz.

scenarios.name: SpaceX fourth force
scenarios.tagline: Convergence creates a new national rival, and value moves from carriers to SpaceX and sellers.
scenarios.summary: Defined as: SpaceX (or another satellite owner) bills at least 3M US mobile lines directly at end-2030, whatever the price level. SpaceX closes EchoStar and Grain on time, wins meaningful upper C-band blocks, and launches a cheap Starlink Mobile plan in 2028 using satellites, 800 MHz and leased towers. By end-2030 it owns over 100 MHz and keeps buying. Prices rise for low-band and satellite-capable bands, where SpaceX and Amazon bid against carriers, while generic mid-band stays near trend. Carriers answer with price cuts and bundles, so service revenue grows only about 1-2% a year and multiples compress.
scenarios.spectrum_prices: Two tiers: low-band and satellite-usable bands clear at $1.5-2.5 or more, and upper C-band clears above $0.94 about half the time. Generic mid-band stays near $0.7-1.2.
scenarios.carriers: Multiples fall toward 5.5-6.5x and the carrier basket lags the S&P 500. Their licences are worth more to others than to them.
scenarios.satellites: SpaceX is the clear winner, and satellite-to-phone revenue reaches the top of our range ($8-12B). Owners of satellite bands (Amazon-Globalstar, AST's L-band rights) gain strategic value.
scenarios.investors: Spectrum exposure works best through the buyer and the sellers: SpaceX itself, EchoStar's SpaceX stake, or pure plays sold into a bidding contest. Incumbent carriers fund the shift rather than benefit from it.
scenarios.signposts: SpaceX qualifies for Auction 115 and wins meaningful blocks (2027); a SpaceX plan launches by mid-2028 at an aggressive price; tower deals covering tens of thousands of sites, or a deal to buy a carrier.
scenarios.forecast_links: q_spacex_subs 3M or more; q_spacex_mhz 100-150+ MHz; b_spacex_retail Yes; b_spacex_ucb Yes; q_ucb_price $0.85-1.35; q_d2d_rev $7-12B; q_ev_ebitda 5.6-6.5x; q_service_rev $246-260B; b_carriers_beat No; b_tech_buys_carrier more likely than its 16% base; b_spacex_top4 still a minority outcome.

scenarios.name: Scarcity premium
scenarios.tagline: Demand outruns supply, and existing holders capture the gains.
scenarios.summary: Defined as: SpaceX bills fewer than 3M US lines directly at end-2030, and the median 2029-30 deal price is $1.40 per MHz-pop or more. Upper C-band clears above the 2021 price, near $1.00-1.35 ($55-72B), as Verizon, AT&T and a bidding SpaceX fight for blocks next to existing C-band. Traffic re-accelerates on AI uplink, glasses and fixed wireless, with at least one year above 25% growth, while 2.7 GHz and 7 GHz slip. Carriers ration fixed wireless and raise prices, so revenue per GB falls more slowly, and the remaining pure plays sell at premiums.
scenarios.spectrum_prices: The median deal price is $1.40 or more, with low-band above $2. New auctions clear near or above 2021 levels.
scenarios.carriers: Pricing power returns, revenue grows 3-4% a year, and multiples re-rate to about 7.5-8.5x. This is the carriers' best chance of beating the S&P 500.
scenarios.satellites: Satellite owners gain as deep-pocketed buyers, but SpaceX stays mainly a wholesale coverage partner rather than a retail rival.
scenarios.investors: This is the only world where both carriers and pure plays win. Even here, gains arrive through sales and auctions rather than steady earnings growth.
scenarios.signposts: CTIA traffic growth above 22% in 2026 or 2027; a measured AI traffic share above 1% by 2028; Auction 115 gross bids above $50B (2027); the 2.7 GHz auction slipping to 2029 or later.

chief.coherence_notes:
No numbers were changed. Every panel aggregate passed the consistency checks, and no lens made a factual error that moved the aggregate. Floating-point noise was rounded (q_ai_share p10 0.42, q_rev_per_gb p90 1.038).

Checks run:
(1) Price times 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz x 335M) gives $22.6B, $41.3B and $72.1B. That matches the proceeds aggregate of $22.5B, $41B and $72.2B.
(2) On the 335M-pop basis the 2021 lower C-band was about $0.87, so the $0.94 threshold needs gross bids of at least $50.4B. A split-lognormal fit to the aggregate price gives P(>$0.94 | auction concludes) of about 32%. Times about 95% that it concludes by end-2028, that is about 31%, which matches b_ucb_above.
(3) Revenue per GB: $266B / 328 EB = $0.81, against the aggregate's $0.80. The range ($0.63-1.04) sits inside the ratio extremes.
(4) Traffic quantiles imply 10.3%, 15.5% and 21.4% a year for 2025-30. That fits b_reaccel at 14% (the P90 is near 21% a year) and b_crunch at 7% (even P10 growth of about 10% stays far above revenue growth). The 2035 median implies about 10% a year after 2030. The AI share median of 1.5% is about 5 EB, which is plausible within 328 EB.
(5) The 2030 new-MHz distribution is lumpy. P10 is upper C-band only (160), P50 is upper C-band plus 2.7 GHz (370), and a total above about 435 needs upper mid-band. A smooth fit gives P(>435) of about 37%, against b_7ghz at 30% plus a small mmWave tail. The lumps explain the gap.
(6) SpaceX subscribers: about 25% at zero fits b_spacex_retail (53% by 2028, about 72% by 2030). P(>3M) is about 23% and P(>5M) about 14%, which supports b_spacex_top4 at 10% once the acquisition route is included.
(7) EV/EBITDA P(>8x) is about 15%, consistent with the 14% scarcity scenario.

Scenarios: they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive by construction. A world goes to s3 if SpaceX (or another satellite owner) bills at least 3M US lines directly at end-2030. Otherwise it is classified by the median 2029-30 deal price: below $0.60 is s2, $0.60-1.40 is s1, and $1.40 or more is s4. If there are no qualifying 2029-30 deals, use the latest qualifying deal price instead.

The weights come from the aggregate distributions. For mid-band, P(<$0.60) is about 26% and P(>$1.40) about 21%. For SpaceX lines, P(>3M) is about 23%, with the price split inside s3 tilted higher (30% above $1.40, 10% below $0.60).

Cross-checks against the scenario weights:
- Implied b_ucb_above is about 32% (panel: 31%).
- Implied b_spacex_retail is about 53% (panel: 53%).
- Implied b_carriers_beat is about 35% (panel: 36%).
s2 and s3 are nearly tied (24 vs 23). Their order is a close call.

Tensions left:
(a) The q_spacex_mhz median of 88 needs a substantive addition beyond the 79 MHz pending to be more likely than not. With b_spacex_ucb at 45%, and some of those wins only token, that depends on other routes: EchoStar's paired AWS-3, the 2020-2025 MHz block and 2.7 GHz. A defensible median runs from about 81 to 88. It was left at the panel value.
(b) The $235B 2025 service revenue base is unverified (other trackers give $255-326B). That affects how q_service_rev and q_rev_per_gb resolve, but not the ratio logic.
(c) T-Mobile no longer discloses its fixed wireless count, which adds noise to q_fwa_2030.
(d) The panel sits below several research-digest medians: AI share 1.5% vs 4%, satellite-to-phone revenue $4.8B vs $6B, SpaceX lines 1M vs 3M, and 6G 49% vs 60%. In each case the panel leaned on the slowing measured data and the record of vendor forecasts overshooting.
(e) The investables section's upper C-band view (about 60% concluding by 2028, $30B median) came from training data and is contradicted by the firm 27 April 2027 schedule. It was correctly given no weight.
